https://www.telegraph.co.uk/music/concer.title: Sex, drugs and teens off the leash: The return of Reading Festival
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/music/concer.subtitle: It has become a post-GCSE rite of passage, but if you think your child is going just to listen to music, think again...
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/music/concer.text:
The stench of burning polyester – that’s my abiding memory of Reading Festival 2007. As the sun came up over a sea of fetid 16-year-olds, half the tents seemed to be on fire. We’d stayed up all night to watch the sunrise, which is not as magical as it sounds when you’re in a field just off the M4 and your wellies stink of the human excrement you stepped in the night before.
I remember looking out at the billows of smoke and turning to survey our camp. My tent, which my parents had given me for my birthday a week before, now had the words: “The girls in this tent want your hot sex” scrawled across it. My friend Sam had gifted us that particular message on day one – every night, we were dive-bombed by passing gangs of lads, leaving the tent half-broken and smeared with mud by Monday morning.
The other tent, a floral number from, inexplicably, Ted Baker (did I mention it was 2007?) stank of vodka, one friend having mistaken a plastic (again – 2007, don’t shoot the millennial) bottle filled with Tesco Imperial vodka for water, taking a giant hungover glug and promptly spraying it over the tent. It was a sorry state of affairs, but even then it didn’t seem worth throwing them in a bonfire.
If this sounds like a seventh circle of hell into which you wouldn’t send your worst enemy let alone your precious sweet 16-year-old, I can understand.
If, however, you are about to go through the time-honoured tradition of waving your child off to Reading Festival this week, sending them into the wilds of Berkshire with a clutch of GCSEs and a sleeping bag, you might want to take a deep breath and read on.
It’s that time of year when Britain’s teenagers flock to Glastonbury’s weird, grungy cousin – ostensibly to listen to indie music, in reality to go entirely feral, many of them for the first time. And they will be paying at least £265 for a ticket. Mention the name to anyone over the age of 30 and they’ll shudder, the memories of what one colleague recalls as one of the most “barbaric” experiences of his youth, still just as vivid years on.
I’d like to tell you the festival has changed, that Generation Z has cleaned up Reading’s act. Surely the youth, who we are always accusing of being puritanical bores, at least have an understanding of the carbon footprint of burning a two-man from Mountain Warehouse? Not so. In fact, it would seem the climate crisis doesn’t exist on the final weekend of August, when your choice is thus: bang on about how you’re totally going to drop out of school and join Just Stop Oil in September, or earn “massive legend” status by lobbing your mate’s tent on the fire.
“These days it’s pretty chill Thursday to Saturday, but then something happens on the Sunday and people become animals,” says one 22-year-old, who experienced her first Reading last summer. “They allow open fires so no one thinks anything of seeing smoke on the site and on the last night people just set their camp on fire. At one point people were throwing bottles of p--s at each other. My friend and I had to hide in our tent.”
Things don’t sound as if they have progressed much since 2008, when one friend recalls watching 200 people form a circle around police officers. “They were performing the hokey cokey in order to block them from stopping the rest of the field setting their tents ablaze.”
While we’re on tents, if they are festival first-timers, do remind your children a tent isn’t like a house with a lock on the front door. One friend arrived back to his in 2010 to find two strangers having sex in it. The second night, someone vomited down the side of it. On the third, someone stole his booze and set the tent on fire. A real hat-trick. Brutal stuff. Character-building though.
One tip from a recent Reading attendee that you might want to pass on: get there early and camp close to the arena – the red campsite, specifically. “The closer to the arena you are the more regulated it is,” she says, “there are more staff watching you.” If, however, the likelihood that your teenager is heading to a festival in search of adult supervision seems, at best, low, you might wish to pick your battles and not bother insisting on that one. Stick to the old faithfuls: drink water, don’t lose your friends, don’t let your phone battery die, don’t smuggle in any class A drugs. You know, the classics.
Google the festival and you’ll get an insight into who makes up the bulk of the clientele – one of the top search terms is “Is Reading safe for 16-year-olds?”. It’s a good question. One mother, whose daughter went last year, marching off without a care in the world after picking up her GCSE results, was among the throng of parents who got that call in the middle of the night, begging for someone to pick them up. “Her tent had become the place where all her friends would take coke. They were getting progressively louder and more sexually adventurous and it was all too much for her.”
Another had to hotfoot it from south London to pick up her son last year. He “felt unsafe” when all his friends were “overdoing it” and asked to come home.
Some things never change, then – one friend recalls calling her dad to ask him to pick her up back in 2012 when her best friend kicked her out of her tent in the rain “so she could have sex in it”. Classy.
If you don’t fancy a panicked call, one old hand recommends arranging to pick up your teens on the Sunday night to avoid the “chaos” of the final few hours of the festival.
And what if you don’t get that SOS call? “You might never know what they got up to,” warns one parent whose daughter went last year. “When I asked the girls what they’d done at Reading there was notably no mention of any music, but nor was there much detail on what else they did. Given they’d all lost their voices and couldn’t get out of bed for a week I think I can imagine and, frankly, I think I’d rather be spared the details.”
That’s another point – expect your teen to come home having dropped an octave or two. Sure, that might be because they were singing along to Billie Eilish so effusively. Or it might be all the passionfruit vapes. Rest assured, if your teen hasn’t yet shown any sign of the smoking habit you likely had at their age, they will have found something else to puff on. Disposable vapes are banned on site but they slip through. Festival sites always used to be covered in cigarette butts; these days, after a set finishes, the field is a “sea of fluorescent vapes”, says one regular. “That age group all vape, they don’t really smoke.” One parent recalls her daughter “leaving home a sweet 16 and coming back sounding like Keith Richards”.
Still, at least they have phones these days, eh? Maybe even an AirTag so you can track their location? Parents warn it might not make a difference. “We didn’t hear from them once,” says one, who recalls desperately restraining herself from texting her daughter at regular intervals to remind her to put on sun cream and drink some water. “I was so worried she was going to get dehydrated.”
I suspect keeping up the H2O may have been low on her list of priorities but it’s a nice thought. Even if you have the full kit, wellies can be stolen – as one festivalgoer reports happened to her, and then her friend borrowed her torch and dropped it down the loo.
So what can you do to ensure your little festival novices, your Covid teens on the brink of freedom, stay as safe as possible? The truth is, not a lot. And perhaps that’s as it should be. You can send them away with some food and a refillable water bottle, but the chances are they are going to be young and foolish however well you have taught them. And, barring major dramas, isn’t that a tiny bit reassuring? Isn’t it a good thing that, in 2023, it is still possible to be 16 and go a little bit feral at a festival? We are always accusing Gen Z of never having any fun, of being too serious, too fearful, too militantly healthy. For this one weekend, then, perhaps it’s time to relinquish all control. Just keep your phone nearby for the inevitable 3am call begging you to drive down the M4 in your dressing gown and rescue them when it all gets too much. Or do as my friend’s mum did 23 years ago – book them a room at the Reading Holiday Inn. At least they’re less likely to burn that down at the end of the weekend than they are a £40 tent.
It seems fitting that the 21-year-old star is closing proceedings on Sunday: Eilish’s spectacular, blackly introspective pop sound has seen her labelled the voice of her angst-ridden, doom-obsessed generation. The crowd will be massive – and stomping tracks like Bad Guy and Happier Than Ever are guaranteed to go down a treat.
Having stepped in to replace Scottish singer Lewis Capaldi, who postponed his summer shows for health reasons, this year will mark the second in a row that the Cheshire indie-band have headlined. Matty Healy and Co will be performing their 2013 self-titled debut in full, though it’s yet to be seen if the divisive frontman will say anything controversial (or tuck into any raw meat) on stage.
The Japanese-British singer is one of the most exciting talents in music, delivering a dizzying mixture of pop, nu-metal, R’n’B, dance and rock. Playing Reading the day after The 1975’s headline set, fans will be waiting with bated breath to see if she delivers another anti-Healy tirade like she did at Glastonbury.
Expect singalongs and Springsteen-esque reflections on everyday life on Friday from the Geordie singer, with the soaring Seventeen Going Under guaranteed to tug at the heartstrings.
Born and raised in West London, the drill rapper will inevitably draw one of the biggest crowds of the weekend when he takes to the stage to power through viral hits like Sprinter and Doja on Saturday. Here’s hoping he brings out some special guests: at Worthy Farm in June, he was joined by Brit Award-winning rapper Dave – and his baby.
The 23-year-old winner of the 2022 Brits Rising Star Award will take to the stage on Saturday, ready to perform her thoughtful, emotionally mature songs to thousands of fans. A talent who will only keep getting bigger and better.
Fresh from supporting indie supergroup boygenius in London, Muna will bring their joyous, anthemic blend of pop and rock to Reading on Sunday. Silk Chiffon, normally performed with Phoebe Bridgers, is sure to be a highlight of the set.
It’s worth it for the Mr Brightside singalong alone. Brandon Flowers’ gang of Las Vegas showboats will power through hits from their seven albums on Saturday night, delighting a new generation of festival-goers with classics like Read My Mind and Spaceman.
Fronted by Elijah Hewson, son of none other than U2 superstar Bono, this Dublin-based indie band have earned a loyal following thanks to their chaotic live shows and thrilling combination of new wave and psychedelic sounds.
Singing about everything from nouveaux riches social climbers to the class system’s grip on British society, the Leeds four-piece are critical darlings and a thrillingly good live band to boot. A welcome dose of good old-fashioned anarchy, amid all the polished pop elsewhere on the bill.
